3:109.ar: وَلِلَّهِ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرۡجَعُ ٱلۡأُمُورُ
3:109.en: Unto Allah belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth; and unto Allah all things are returned

3:110.ar: كُنتُمۡ خَيۡرَ أُمَّةٍ أُخۡرِجَتۡ لِلنَّاسِ تَأۡمُرُونَ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَتَنۡهَوۡنَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَتُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِۗ وَلَوۡ ءَامَنَ أَهۡلُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ لَكَانَ خَيۡرࣰ ا لَّهُمۚ مِّنۡهُمُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَأَكۡثَرُهُمُ ٱلۡفَٰسِقُونَ
3:110.en: Ye are the best community that hath been raised up for mankind. Ye enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency; and ye believe in Allah. And if the People of the Scripture had believed it had been better for them. Some of them are believers; but most of them are evil-livers

3:111.ar: لَن يَضُرُّوكُمۡ إِلَّآ أَذࣰ ىۖ وَإِن يُقَٰتِلُوكُمۡ يُوَلُّوكُمُ ٱلۡأَدۡبَارَ ثُمَّ لَا يُنصَرُونَ
3:111.en: They will not harm you save a trifling hurt, and if they fight against you they will turn and flee. And afterward they will not be helped

3:112.ar: ضُرِبَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلذِّلَّةُ أَيۡنَ مَا ثُقِفُوٓاْ إِلَّا بِحَبۡلࣲ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَحَبۡلࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَبَآءُو بِغَضَبࣲ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَضُرِبَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡمَسۡكَنَةُۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ يَكۡفُرُونَ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَيَقۡتُلُونَ ٱلۡأَنۢبِيَآءَ بِغَيۡرِ حَقࣲّۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِمَا عَصَواْ وَّكَانُواْ يَعۡتَدُونَ
3:112.en: Ignominy shall be their portion wheresoever they are found save (where they grasp) a rope from Allah and a rope from men. They have incurred anger from their Lord, and wretchedness is laid upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve the revelations of Allah, and slew the prophets wrongfully. That is because they were rebellious and used to transgress

3:113.ar: ۞لَيۡسُواْ سَوَآءࣰۗ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ أُمَّةࣱ قَآئِمَةࣱ يَتۡلُونَ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ءَانَآءَ ٱلَّيۡلِ وَهُمۡ يَسۡجُدُونَ
3:113.en: They are not all alike. Of the People of the Scripture there is a staunch community who recite the revelations of Allah in the night season, falling prostrate (before Him)

3:114.ar: يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِ وَيَأۡمُرُونَ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَيَنۡهَوۡنَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَيُسَٰرِعُونَ فِي ٱلۡخَيۡرَٰتِۖ وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
3:114.en: They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency, and vie one with another in good works. These are of the righteous

3:115.ar: وَمَا يَفۡعَلُواْ مِنۡ خَيۡرࣲ فَلَن يُكۡفَرُوهُۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِٱلۡمُتَّقِينَ
3:115.en: And whatever good they do, they will not be denied the meed thereof. Allah is Aware of those who ward off (evil)

3:116.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لَن تُغۡنِيَ عَنۡهُمۡ أَمۡوَٰلُهُمۡ وَلَآ أَوۡلَٰدُهُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ شَيۡـࣰٔ اۖ وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِۖ هُمۡ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
3:116.en: Lo! the riches and the progeny of those who disbelieve will not avail them aught against Allah; and such are rightful owners of the Fire. They will abide therein

3:117.ar: مَثَلُ مَا يُنفِقُونَ فِي هَٰذِهِ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا كَمَثَلِ رِيحࣲ فِيهَا صِرٌّ أَصَابَتۡ حَرۡثَ قَوۡمࣲ ظَلَمُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ فَأَهۡلَكَتۡهُۚ وَمَا ظَلَمَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَلَٰكِنۡ أَنفُسَهُمۡ يَظۡلِمُونَ
3:117.en: The likeness of that which they spend in this life of the world is as the likeness of a biting, icy wind which smiteth the harvest of a people who have wronged themselves, and devastateth it. Allah wronged them not, but they do wrong themselves

3:118.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَتَّخِذُواْ بِطَانَةࣰ مِّن دُونِكُمۡ لَا يَأۡلُونَكُمۡ خَبَالࣰ ا وَدُّواْ مَا عَنِتُّمۡ قَدۡ بَدَتِ ٱلۡبَغۡضَآءُ مِنۡ أَفۡوَٰهِهِمۡ وَمَا تُخۡفِي صُدُورُهُمۡ أَكۡبَرُۚ قَدۡ بَيَّنَّا لَكُمُ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِۖ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡقِلُونَ
3:118.en: O ye who believe! Take not for intimates others than your own folk, who would spare no pains to ruin you; they love to hamper you. Hatred is revealed by (the utterance of) their mouths, but that which their breasts hide is greater. We have made plain for you the revelations if ye will understand

3:119.ar: هَٰٓأَنتُمۡ أُوْلَآءِ تُحِبُّونَهُمۡ وَلَا يُحِبُّونَكُمۡ وَتُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱلۡكِتَٰبِ كُلِّهِۦ وَإِذَا لَقُوكُمۡ قَالُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا وَإِذَا خَلَوۡاْ عَضُّواْ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡأَنَامِلَ مِنَ ٱلۡغَيۡظِۚ قُلۡ مُوتُواْ بِغَيۡظِكُمۡۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
3:119.en: Lo! ye are those who love them though they love you not, and ye believe in all the Scripture. When they fall in with you they say: We believe; but when they go apart they bite their finger-tips at you, for rage. Say: Perish in your rage! Lo! Allah is Aware of what is hidden in (your) breasts

3:120.ar: إِن تَمۡسَسۡكُمۡ حَسَنَةࣱ تَسُؤۡهُمۡ وَإِن تُصِبۡكُمۡ سَيِّئَةࣱ يَفۡرَحُواْ بِهَاۖ وَإِن تَصۡبِرُواْ وَتَتَّقُواْ لَا يَضُرُّكُمۡ كَيۡدُهُمۡ شَيۡـًٔاۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا يَعۡمَلُونَ مُحِيطࣱ‏
3:120.en: If a lucky chance befall you, it is evil unto them, and if disaster strike you they rejoice thereat. But if ye persevere and keep from evil their guile will never harm you. Lo! Allah is Surrounding what they do

73:5.ar: إِنَّا سَنُلۡقِي عَلَيۡكَ قَوۡلࣰ ا ثَقِيلًا
73:5.en: For we shall charge thee with a word of weight

4:157.ar: وَقَوۡلِهِمۡ إِنَّا قَتَلۡنَا ٱلۡمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبۡنَ مَرۡيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمۡۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخۡتَلَفُواْ فِيهِ لَفِي شَكࣲّ مِّنۡهُۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنۡ عِلۡمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينَۢا
4:157.en: And because of their saying: We slew the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, Allah's messenger - they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them; and lo! those who disagree concerning it are in doubt thereof; they have no knowledge thereof save pursuit of a conjecture; they slew him not for certain

2A0ffGUJyNY.speaker: adnan
2A0ffGUJyNY.speaker_note: continues his nightly reflections with verse voting and his slides; recalls his own teacher
2A0ffGUJyNY.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 3: Quranic Reflections (Al-Baqarah 267 to Al 'Imran 120)
2A0ffGUJyNY.one_line: Al-Baqarah's closing verse on capacity, Al 'Imran's external and internal challenges, choosing your inner circle, Isa and end-times passivity, and love proven by following.
2A0ffGUJyNY.summary: He closes Al-Baqarah and introduces Al 'Imran as a manual for protecting the deen from external challenges, in its first hundred verses, and internal ones, through Uhud in the second half, insisting that problems must be acknowledged before they can be treated and that Muslims in the West can keep their identity while integrating. The final verse of Al-Baqarah comforts those weighed down by the surah's demands: Allah asks nothing beyond your capacity but everything within it, and the closing dua is an attitude to live by. He presses people to find their full capacity instead of worrying about, or cursing, what they cannot influence. On the warning against taking outsiders as close counsel, he urges choosing an inner circle that truly wants you to succeed, even beyond themselves, and leaving anyone's circle if you envy them. On Allah raising Isa, he explains the majority view, notes there is no consensus, and argues that disputed and end-times matters should not occupy ordinary Muslims, because such narrations breed passivity while Gaza bleeds; you are the one being waited for. Finally, love for Allah is proven by following the Prophet, and Allah answers with forgiveness, since love is only as good as its consequences.

outline.heading: Opening
Al-Baqarah: the longest surah and the simplest to grasp
outline.gist: It has two parts: your job as khalifah and caregiver, and the method of Islam that covers nearly every aspect of the deen.

outline.heading: The chapters of fiqh follow Al-Baqarah's topics
outline.gist: Tonight continues with wealth, usury and loans before the conclusion.

outline.heading: The conclusion: listen, obey, try your best, seek forgiveness
outline.gist: The closing verses say all belongs to Allah, the prophets before you obeyed, you are asked only to do your best and to ask forgiveness for mistakes.

outline.heading: Al 'Imran: protecting the deen from external challenges
outline.gist: Every ideology faces opposition from people and groups outside it.

outline.heading: Internal challenges: the mistakes of the believers
outline.gist: The second kind of challenge comes from the followers themselves.

outline.heading: The first hundred verses: challenges from outside
outline.gist: The surah splits almost exactly in half, the first part dealing with what affects Muslims' ability to function from outside.

outline.heading: The second half: Uhud, a purely internal failure
outline.gist: The defeat came not from the enemy's strength but from the Muslims' own mistakes, which the surah examines so they are not repeated.

outline.heading: We are living the same situation today
outline.gist: We face external challenges, but most of our challenges are internal.

outline.heading: Why he complains: problems left unaddressed
outline.gist: Challenges stare us in the face while we look away and work around them; we cannot progress without naming them.

outline.heading: You cannot treat a patient who denies the disease
outline.gist: As a doctor cannot help someone who will not accept he is ill, the ummah must first acknowledge its problems.

outline.heading: Intellectual challenges: doubts from outside
outline.gist: External sources poke holes in your faith and the surah shows how to respond.

outline.heading: Temptation challenges
outline.gist: Desires for the forbidden, whether substances or sexual, that come at you from outside.

outline.heading: Advice for facing external challenges
outline.gist: Piety, unity, social reform, confidence, objectivity, awareness and caution, after which the internal challenges begin.

outline.heading: Muslims in the West: the identity challenge
outline.gist: Surrounded by people who do not share our faith and may wish we gave it up, we must hold on to who we are.

outline.heading: The tolerance challenge: integrating with those who differ
outline.gist: We still have to be part of the country we live in and deal productively with people unlike us.

outline.heading: You need not lose either
outline.gist: Some keep a strong identity but cannot work with others, others integrate and forget who they are; both can be held together.

outline.heading: Interlude
The closing verse brings comfort after a heavy surah
outline.gist: After setting out your job and your method, Al-Baqarah ends with a verse meant to reassure.

outline.heading: His teacher: if Al-Baqarah does not cost you sleep, you have not understood it
outline.gist: First it should frighten you with what is asked, and only its last two verses let you sleep.

outline.heading: The weight of the responsibility
outline.gist: A juz and a half of rulings, reforms and changes you must hold yourself to and carry to the world.

outline.heading: A heavy word: even the companions did not grasp its weight
outline.gist: The Prophet was told at the start that he would receive a heavy word; no one fully realized how much work it would be.

outline.heading: Spreading it and practising it well enough to be accepted
outline.gist: The message had to go from an unknown corner of the world to every corner, lived well enough that people would accept it.

outline.heading: Enter the verse with your guard up
outline.gist: Only someone who feels the burden the surah builds will hear this verse speak to him.

outline.heading: Nothing beyond your capacity, but everything within it
outline.gist: Allah never holds you to what you could not have done, yet asks for all that lies within your humanity.

outline.heading: Each soul earns what it worked for
outline.gist: You are rewarded for what you strive toward and accountable for your mistakes.

outline.heading: Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err
outline.gist: Allah commands this dua because forgetting and mistakes are certain for every human.

outline.heading: Do not burden us as You burdened those before us
outline.gist: Asking not to carry the heavy burdens and sins of earlier peoples, nor what we cannot bear.

outline.heading: Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy, grant us victory
outline.gist: You acknowledge Him as your only Lord and ask for success over those who oppose you.

outline.heading: The dua is an attitude to live by
outline.gist: Many duas of the Quran are meant to be lived, not only recited: trying your best and asking pardon for shortcomings.

outline.heading: What we lack: people running at full capacity
outline.gist: We need people who know they are responsible for everything within their reach and work hard on it.

outline.heading: Stop worrying about what you cannot influence
outline.gist: Too many talk about matters far beyond their reach while neglecting what is within it.

outline.heading: Muslims in the West: what is your capacity?
outline.gist: Have you worked out what you can actually do, and are you doing it?

outline.heading: Cursing corrupt rulers is an escape from our capacity
outline.gist: It is easier and more fun to curse rulers who do not know we exist than to fulfil our own capacity.

outline.heading: Bitanah: your close counsel
outline.gist: Among the external challenges, Allah warns about the inner circle: the people you turn to in need, distress or for quality time.

outline.heading: Watch who you choose for your inner circle
outline.gist: Whether or not you call them that, these people are your bitanah, so choose carefully.

outline.heading: The word: what touches you from the inside
outline.gist: Bitanah comes from the inner lining, the people close enough to influence your decisions and direction.

outline.heading: You need close people; loneliness is not the answer
outline.gist: Having an inner circle is necessary; someone living without one needs help.

outline.heading: Not those who long to see you fall
outline.gist: Exclude people who spare no effort to weaken you, whose hatred shows in their words while their hearts hide worse.

outline.heading: Choose people who truly love you
outline.gist: At ten or at seventy, everyone has close counsel; choose those who want the best for you, not those who merely enable you.

outline.heading: Most people want your success, as long as it is not more than theirs
outline.gist: Such a person does not belong in your inner circle.

outline.heading: If you feel that way about someone, leave his circle
outline.gist: Be close only to those you want to see shine beyond you, which takes a selflessness and love most people lack.

outline.heading: Rare people who are happy to be outgrown
outline.gist: Parents, and sometimes siblings, pray you become stronger than them.

outline.heading: A teacher fails if his student does not surpass him
outline.gist: Knowledge must expand from generation to generation, so a good teacher wants you to know more than he does.

outline.heading: Interlude
Other faiths as an external challenge: an entangled story
outline.gist: Christianity and Judaism are the faiths we deal with most, and our stories of Musa, Isa, Dawud, Yaqub and Ibrahim overlap with theirs yet differ.

outline.heading: End-times beliefs in politics
outline.gist: Christian and Jewish ideas of Armageddon shape politics behind closed doors, and many of today's problems come from a skewed version of that story.

outline.heading: Isa raised, purified, his followers made superior
outline.gist: Allah tells Isa He will take him back, raise him, cleanse him of the disbelievers and judge between all on the Day.

outline.heading: Isa was raised before death and not crucified
outline.gist: Most scholars hold he was raised alive; he was certainly not killed and someone else was on the cross.

outline.heading: Believing in his return without building life around it
outline.gist: Like Christians and Jews we believe the Messiah returns, but we are not required to prepare for it or wait on it.

outline.heading: Some scholars held he died: there is no consensus
outline.gist: He thinks the majority is correct, but the difference of opinion matters.

outline.heading: Disputed matters are not first-degree theology
outline.gist: Focus on what no scholar disputes: your role, ethics and the agreed rituals.

outline.heading: A century spent on the undebatable would serve us best
outline.gist: Preaching humility, sincerity, honesty and trustworthiness, and leaving controversy aside.

outline.heading: What the Quran tells us about Isa is all we need
outline.gist: What is essential the Quran at least points to for the Prophet to explain; what it does not mention we can live without.

outline.heading: Do not begin, or end, with end-times narrations
outline.gist: Detailed study of the end of time belongs to specialists in historical texts; ordinary learners are easily confused by it.

outline.heading: End-times stories make people passive spectators
outline.gist: People treat the end of days like a film they watch with popcorn and feel less obliged to contribute.

outline.heading: Thirty thousand dead and nothing happened
outline.gist: Passivity means nothing moves, and if the Ka'bah itself were attacked it would be destroyed while people wait.

outline.heading: You are the one being waited for
outline.gist: Your job is to carry the message, practise and teach it, and unite people upon it.

outline.heading: Study the Quran and the Prophet's life first
outline.gist: With his proactive mentality you can read those narrations without losing your drive; otherwise you wait on the couch for someone else to fix things.

outline.heading: Interlude
If you love Allah, follow me
outline.gist: The verse can be read two ways; taken as worded, following the Prophet is the testament of loving Allah.

outline.heading: The Prophet lived exactly as Allah loves
outline.gist: Not out of pride but to teach: do not go beyond or below how he lived.

outline.heading: Love is known by its effects, not its definition
outline.gist: Love is hard to define, but its consequences and behaviours can be seen.

outline.heading: Allah loves you back, in a rising cycle
outline.gist: He already showed love by creating you; following the Prophet earns more of His love, which deepens yours, until it brings you to Paradise.

outline.heading: He shows His love by forgiving your sins
outline.gist: Your love is defined by following the Prophet; His is shown in forgiveness.

outline.heading: 'I love you' with a slap means nothing
outline.gist: Words of love paired with harm are worse than useless.

outline.heading: Spouses show love through what they do
outline.gist: Husbands show it by sacrificing for their families all their lives, and wives in their care for everyone, though they also say it more.

outline.heading: Love with no consequences has no value
outline.gist: Someone who says he loves you but never shows up when you are in need offers nothing.

outline.heading: No one cares what is in your heart but you
outline.gist: What counts is that you make dua for someone, help him, do not envy him, and pick him up and cover him when he falls.

outline.heading: Saying you love Allah is easy; He asks you to show it
outline.gist: Follow His most beloved and He will show His love by removing all your sins.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran: reading, reflecting, living it
themes.note: Al-Baqarah sets out the job and the method, and Al 'Imran shows how to protect the deen from outside and inside.

themes.label: Reform (islah)
themes.note: Reform starts with acknowledging internal problems, as a patient must accept the diagnosis.

themes.label: Muslim identity and life in the West / Canada
themes.note: Muslims in the West must hold both a firm identity and constructive integration rather than swinging between them.

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Allah holds each soul to its full capacity and no more; the closing dua is the attitude of someone trying his best.

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: The dua at the end of Al-Baqarah is commanded so that every Muslim makes it and lives by it.

themes.label: Agency, responsibility and rejecting victim mentality
themes.note: Focus on what you can influence and work at full capacity instead of complaining about what you cannot change.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Choose an inner circle that truly wants your success, and be that kind of friend to others.

themes.label: Envy, anger and other diseases of the heart
themes.note: Many people support your success only until it exceeds theirs; such envy disqualifies them from your inner circle.

themes.label: Stories of earlier prophets
themes.note: Isa was raised and not crucified; his return is believed by most but is not a matter to build one's life around.

themes.label: Priorities in the deen: fundamentals before details
themes.note: Spend effort on undisputed ethics and basics rather than controversial or non-essential topics.

themes.label: Agency, responsibility and rejecting victim mentality
themes.note: End-times speculation breeds passivity; Muslims must act instead of waiting for someone to come and fix things.

themes.label: Palestine, Gaza and the suffering of Muslims
themes.note: Tens of thousands killed in Gaza while the ummah remains passive.

themes.label: Love: of Allah, the Prophet, and one another
themes.note: Love is shown through actions: love of Allah through following the Prophet, His love through forgiveness, and human love through care.

themes.label: Marriage and the relationship between spouses
themes.note: Spouses show love mainly through sacrifice and care rather than words.

quran.point: The Prophet was told at the start he would receive a heavy word, the weight of the responsibility.
Isa was not killed or crucified; someone else was made to resemble him.

maxims: Nothing beyond your capacity, but everything within it
You can't treat a patient who denies the disease
If you don't become better than me, I failed
You are what is being waited for
Love is only as good as its consequences

stories.point: The defeat was entirely internal, which makes it the model for addressing a community's own mistakes.
If the surah does not frighten you out of sleep you have not understood it; only its last verses let you rest.
Know what the Quran says and leave the speculative details aside.

contemporary: End-times beliefs shaping politics and discussed among members of the US Congress
Gaza: about 30,000 killed while the ummah stays passive
Muslims in the West balancing identity and integration
Complaining about corrupt rulers in Muslim countries
Netflix and couch culture as a picture of passivity
takeaways: Name and acknowledge the community's internal problems so they can be fixed.
Work out your full capacity and act on it instead of worrying about what you cannot influence.
Choose an inner circle that truly wants you to succeed, and step out of anyone's circle if you envy him.
Focus on the Quran, the Prophet's life and agreed ethics rather than end-times speculation.
Prove your love for Allah by following the Prophet, and show love to people through what you do.

TUvLTMqLc9k.speaker: adnan
TUvLTMqLc9k.speaker_note: teaches his yearly English fiqh of Ramadan class in his masjid; mentions his medical residency
TUvLTMqLc9k.title: Fiqh of Ramadan (Ramadan Prep Series)
TUvLTMqLc9k.one_line: A practical walk through the rulings of Ramadan fasting: intention, what breaks and does not break the fast, exemptions, expiations, sunnahs, tarawih, zakat al-fitr and Eid.
TUvLTMqLc9k.summary: In his yearly fiqh of Ramadan class he gives the majority positions of the four schools rather than one madhab, noting that the schools evolve and that a follower may take the local imam's madhab for Ramadan. He starts with intention: the Ramadan fast needs an intention before dawn, and waking for suhoor is enough, though he finds the Maliki view of one intention for the whole month reasonable. His general rule is that anything taken in intentionally that counts medically as nourishment breaks the fast. He lists the six agreed invalidators, the things that do not break the fast, and the disputed cases such as inhalers, drops, IV lines and suppositories, giving his own view and repeating that health comes before ritual. He covers who may break the fast (the ill, travellers, pregnant and nursing women, the severely fatigued), the duty to make up days before the next Ramadan, and when children should begin fasting. He explains the major and minor expiations with current dollar amounts and who owes them, including the terminally ill and the elderly, and the manners expected of those who cannot fast. He closes with the sunnahs of suhoor and iftar, fasting from sin, staying through tarawih, zakat al-fitr and holding one Eid prayer per community.

outline.heading: Opening
Why learn the rulings, and whose opinions he gives
outline.gist: Children should learn the rulings early and adults need them to explain Ramadan and help the ill and elderly. He gives majority positions across the four schools, notes that schools evolve over time, and says a madhab follower may adopt the local imam's madhab for Ramadan.

outline.heading: The intention for the Ramadan fast
outline.gist: A voluntary fast can be intended mid-morning, but Ramadan and make-up fasts need an intention before dawn; it need not be spoken and waking for suhoor counts. He favours the Maliki view that one intention covers the whole month.

outline.heading: The general rule: intentional nourishment breaks the fast
outline.gist: Anything taken into the body intentionally that meets the medical definition of nourishment invalidates the fast; knowing this spares people panic over every small question.

outline.heading: Invalidator: eating and drinking on purpose
outline.gist: Breaking a Ramadan day deliberately, often out of anger or a fit of temper, is a major sin; the day is made up and repentance accepted, but the reward of that obligatory day can never be regained.

outline.heading: Invalidator: intercourse or its equivalent
outline.gist: Relations between spouses during the day, or deliberately reaching orgasm, break the fast and carry a heavy expiation.

outline.heading: Invalidator: deliberate vomiting
outline.gist: Making oneself vomit breaks the fast; someone who feels sick should first intend to break the fast under the illness exemption and then vomit. He offers help to anyone struggling with bulimia.

outline.heading: Invalidator: parenteral nourishment
outline.gist: Nourishment by IV, under the skin or into the muscle breaks the fast; in hospital, ask whether what you were given was nourishment. Vitamins do not count.

outline.heading: Invalidator: smoking and vaping
outline.gist: Any form of smoking, including shisha and vaping, breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Invalidator: menstruation or childbirth
outline.gist: If bleeding begins even a moment before maghrib, that day is lost and must be repeated. He recaps the six agreed invalidators.

outline.heading: Does not break: brushing teeth and miswak
outline.gist: Brushing or using miswak is fine as long as toothpaste is not swallowed.

outline.heading: Does not break: eating or drinking forgetfully
outline.gist: Allah simply fed the forgetful person. If you see someone eating forgetfully, let them finish rather than reminding them mid-swallow and ruining their fast, unless they are plainly not fasting.

outline.heading: Does not break: a wet dream
outline.gist: A wet dream during a daytime nap does not affect the fast, and one at night only requires ghusl before praying.

outline.heading: Does not break: non-nourishing injections; caution for diabetics
outline.gist: B12, antibiotics, insulin, flu shots and vaccines given into muscle or under the skin are fine. Diabetics must ask their physician weeks before Ramadan whether they can fast; as a resident he saw elderly patients return repeatedly with dangerous sugar levels.

outline.heading: Does not break: swallowing one's own saliva
outline.gist: Swallowing saliva does not break the fast, even if deliberately collected, though doing so is distasteful.

outline.heading: Does not break: water left after wudu
outline.gist: Rinsing the mouth vigorously is disliked while fasting, but there is no need to be obsessive; whatever drops remain after a normal wudu are forgiven. Fasting rests on knowing what you are doing and why.

outline.heading: Disputed: inhalers
outline.gist: Scholars differ; he sees no problem with using an inhaler as needed for asthma, COPD or other lung disease.

outline.heading: Disputed: eye and ear drops
outline.gist: He holds that medical drops do not break the fast, treating a stray drop like the water left after wudu, since none of it is nourishment.

outline.heading: Disputed: non-nourishing IV infusions
outline.gist: IV antibiotics, chemotherapy or dialysis come in fluid that fills the vascular system, which is how hydration is defined, so he holds that any IV breaks the fast. Others disagree, and preserving health always takes priority over the ritual.

outline.heading: Disputed: suppositories
outline.gist: His view is that any suppository breaks the fast regardless of its content, and someone sick enough to need one should usually break the fast anyway.

outline.heading: Pills by mouth: no opinion permits them
outline.gist: Anything swallowed breaks the fast by consensus. Most twice or three-times-daily medications can be shifted to suhoor and iftar; otherwise the patient switches to an injectable form or takes the exemption.

outline.heading: Exemption: illness
outline.gist: Fever, pain or nausea allow breaking the fast, and with a valid excuse the reward of the day is not lost but held until it is made up after Ramadan.

outline.heading: Exemption: travel
outline.gist: He is lenient on shortening and combining prayers but stricter on fasting: at least 82 km, the travel day itself is clear, and longer stays need care because missed days are hard to make up. A trucker who is always on the road technically need not fast but would pile up days to repay.

outline.heading: Exemption: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: Pregnant and nursing women may break the fast without blame, with an expiation caveat he returns to later.

outline.heading: Exemption: severe fatigue
outline.gist: A Syrian refugee doing construction under eighteen-hour Scandinavian summer days asked what to do: intend to fast every day and break only when fatigue becomes harmful, then make it up later. These are judgments between the person and Allah, not for others to police.

outline.heading: Make up missed days before the next Ramadan
outline.gist: Delaying past the next Ramadan is sinful, requires repentance and an expiation, and the day is still owed.

outline.heading: Children: puberty and training to fast
outline.gist: Fasting becomes obligatory at puberty, but children should be trained beforehand so the first year is not crushing, without forcing those too young or making them hate it.

outline.heading: Kinds of maturity and when to start
outline.gist: Physical, social, financial and mental maturity used to arrive together, as with his grandparents who married at thirteen and fourteen. His own view is to start when a child has the physical maturity and self-control fasting needs, usually around nine or ten.

outline.heading: Major expiation: when it is owed
outline.gist: There is consensus that it is owed for intercourse during a Ramadan day; for deliberate eating and drinking the schools differ, and he holds it applies.

outline.heading: Major expiation: what it involves
outline.gist: In sequence: freeing a slave, which no longer applies, then sixty consecutive days of fasting, then feeding sixty poor people, about twelve hundred dollars today. He prefers caution in obligatory matters.

outline.heading: Minor expiation and the chronically ill
outline.gist: The minor expiation is feeding one poor person per day, about twenty dollars. People with illnesses that will not improve, such as dialysis, diabetes or medication every few hours by mouth, pay it for each day and do not fast.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: the elderly
outline.gist: Frail elderly people need not fast and pay per day instead; there is no fixed age. He agrees with scholars who say children pay it for parents who cannot afford it.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: delaying make-up days
outline.gist: Days not made up before the next Ramadan need repentance and one expiation per day, paid once only no matter how many years pass, and the day itself is still owed.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: Days missed for pregnancy or nursing carry an expiation even when made up on time; he advises paying it up front. The husband pays it, while any further expiation for late make-up comes from the wife's own wealth.

outline.heading: Manners for those who cannot fast
outline.gist: Someone exempt, like his friend with familial Mediterranean fever or an elderly patient told not to fast, takes only what is needed away from people's sight and joins the family at iftar rather than eating openly.

outline.heading: Debts of the deceased
outline.gist: Expiations a person owed are paid from their estate, but the overwhelming majority hold that no one can fast on another's behalf. Better to pay during life than leave it to a will.

outline.heading: Late suhoor, early iftar
outline.gist: Fast exactly from dawn to sunset; prolonging it out of misguided piety is not more beloved to Allah.

outline.heading: Do not overeat at suhoor or iftar
outline.gist: Let the stomach shrink; half a litre to a litre of water is plenty, extra just fills the bladder, and salty or sugary food draws water and makes thirst worse.

outline.heading: Breaking the fast on dates or water
outline.gist: The sunnah is fresh dates, then dried dates, then water, in odd numbers.

outline.heading: Dua at iftar
outline.gist: The fasting person has an unrejected dua around the time of breaking the fast. Break it right at the adhan with a sip or a date, pray, then eat.

outline.heading: Fast from sin
outline.gist: It makes no sense to give up food and drink and keep watching, hearing and speaking what is haram; Ramadan moves the line further from haram, not closer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Tarawih: the measure is Quran, not rakah count
outline.gist: Attend a tarawih that completes the Quran at least once; the Prophet prayed eight, eleven or thirteen and the schools differ, so the number never mattered, only the recitation and presence of heart.

outline.heading: Stay until the imam finishes
outline.gist: Young people especially should stand the whole prayer; people who stand in line for hours for a licence suddenly ache everywhere at salah. Praying in congregation strengthens community bonds.

outline.heading: Tarawih means rest: use the breaks
outline.gist: The name comes from resting between sets; if tired, sit out a rakah, read along or pray seated, but stay to the end. You will always regret not pushing a little more.

outline.heading: Interlude
Zakat al-fitr: amount and timing
outline.gist: About twenty dollars a person with inflation; opinions range from the first day of Ramadan, and he favours giving it about a week before Eid so it reaches those in need.

outline.heading: Paying zakat al-fitr in cash
outline.gist: Giving money rather than food is a valid opinion held within the schools, and the yearly dispute over it is not a big deal.

outline.heading: Who pays zakat al-fitr for whom
outline.gist: The breadwinner pays for himself and everyone he supports, including a fetus past 120 days.

outline.heading: Eid prayer outdoors, one per community
outline.gist: The sunnah is an outdoor prayer with whole families attending; a city needs one or two Eid prayers at most, not dozens, since the point is the community gathering.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Ramadan: preparation, fasting, making the most of it
themes.note: A complete practical guide to fasting Ramadan correctly, from intention to Eid.

themes.label: Jurisprudence rulings and how to approach fiqh
themes.note: Gives majority positions across the schools, separates consensus from disputed issues, and states his own preference with reasons, often using medical definitions.

themes.label: Visiting the sick, caring for elders and the vulnerable
themes.note: The chronically ill and elderly should pay expiation instead of fasting against medical advice, and children may pay for parents.

themes.label: Visiting the sick, caring for elders and the vulnerable
themes.note: Diabetic and elderly patients risk their lives fasting without medical clearance.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Train children to fast before puberty according to their capacity, without forcing them or making them hate it.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: Tarawih is about Quran and presence of heart, not rakah count; stay with the imam to the end and use the rest breaks.

themes.label: Moderation and balance (wasatiyyah)
themes.note: No extra piety by fasting longer than required, and no overeating at suhoor or iftar.

themes.label: Sins, their causes and remedies
themes.note: Fasting from food while continuing in haram speech and sights misses the point of the fast.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah
themes.note: One community should gather for one Eid prayer.

The Prophet broke his fast on fresh dates, or dried dates if none, or sips of water.
The fasting person has a dua that is not rejected at the time of breaking the fast.
Whoever does not abandon false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink.
The Prophet's night prayer was eight, eleven or thirteen rakahs.
The Prophet held the Eid prayer outdoors with women, children and whole families attending.

takeaways: Learn the basic rulings of fasting so you can answer your own questions and help others.
Ill, diabetic or elderly relatives should check with their physician and pay the daily expiation rather than fast against medical advice.
Make up missed days before the next Ramadan, and pay the pregnancy or breastfeeding expiation up front.
Keep suhoor and iftar light, break the fast on dates or water with dua, and fast from sin as well as food.
Stay with the imam to the end of tarawih, sitting or resting if needed, and give zakat al-fitr about a week before Eid.

9:111.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱشۡتَرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلَهُم بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۚ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَقۡتُلُونَ وَيُقۡتَلُونَۖ وَعۡدًا عَلَيۡهِ حَقࣰّ ا فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِ وَٱلۡإِنجِيلِ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ وَمَنۡ أَوۡفَىٰ بِعَهۡدِهِۦ مِنَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَٱسۡتَبۡشِرُواْ بِبَيۡعِكُمُ ٱلَّذِي بَايَعۡتُم بِهِۦۚ وَذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
9:111.en: Lo! Allah hath bought from the believers their lives and their wealth because the Garden will be theirs: they shall fight in the way of Allah and shall slay and be slain. It is a promise which is binding on Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. Who fulfilleth His covenant better than Allah? Rejoice then in your bargain that ye have made, for that is the supreme triumph

20:83.en: And (it was said): What hath made thee hasten from thy folk, O Moses

20:84.ar: قَالَ هُمۡ أُوْلَآءِ عَلَىٰٓ أَثَرِي وَعَجِلۡتُ إِلَيۡكَ رَبِّ لِتَرۡضَىٰ
20:84.en: He said: They are close upon my track. I hastened unto Thee, my Lord, that Thou mightest be well pleased

WsB0lW-MW04.speaker: adnan
WsB0lW-MW04.speaker_note: his interactive pre-Ramadan session at his centre; describes his own Ramadan routine, teachers and childhood masjid
WsB0lW-MW04.title: Ramadan Prep: Making It the Best Ramadan Ever
WsB0lW-MW04.one_line: Working through the audience's own obstacles and goals, he gives practical and spiritual steps to make the coming Ramadan the best ever.
WsB0lW-MW04.summary: Every Ramadan should be treated as possibly the last, and this one carries extra weight after months of suffering in the Holy Land, so he asks people to make becoming better for the suffering their umbrella intention. Working from audience responses, he diagnoses the obstacles: work and school pressures point to missing routine, so write out a schedule for the month; laziness, loneliness and commuting point to missing companions; long shifts and poor sleep call for pushing limits without breaking. Asked why they want change, people name repentance, Paradise and a reset, which he links to Ramadan as a taste of Paradise in this life and a turning point in Muslim history. He insists on what each person controls: strong will comes from environment, eating less makes the night prayer enjoyable, and the nearest masjid is the one you will keep attending. He ranks priorities: the Quran, since Ramadan draws its status from it; presence with Allah, which does not come cheap; and community, because Islam is a team effort. His closing points are repentance from a whole way of life, dedicating oneself as an endowment for Allah, volunteering with the intention that preserves the reward of prayer, finding joy in giving, investing in salah, and fasting with every limb, ending with Musa hastening to please his Lord.

outline.heading: Opening
Make it your best: it may be your last
outline.gist: Come in enthusiastic and optimistic each year; no one knows which Ramadan is their last, and each one done this way becomes memorable in its own way.

outline.heading: This year's motivation: the Holy Land
outline.gist: After months of what has happened to Muslims in Gaza, Ramadan must be a turning point, with the umbrella intention of becoming better for all who suffer.

outline.heading: What gets in the way
outline.gist: The audience names work, school, exams, laziness, social media, lack of will, loneliness and food as their obstacles.

outline.heading: Missing routine: write a schedule
outline.gist: Most obstacles are a lack of routine; write out each day of the month around classes and work, as he did for years before his own routine settled.

outline.heading: Missing companions
outline.gist: Laziness, loneliness and long commutes come down to lacking good company; find people who will call you and bring you along, and let regulars welcome newcomers.

outline.heading: Push your limits without breaking
outline.gist: Long hours and night shifts may cost some nights, but challenge yourself; you can survive on less sleep than you think.

outline.heading: Sleep and mothers
outline.gist: He manages on four or five hours plus a nap; mothers have it hardest with no days off from their children.

outline.heading: Following the prayer remotely
outline.gist: He accepts following the masjid's prayer remotely within the city for mothers, the elderly and the sick who cannot attend or recite themselves.

outline.heading: Repentance as motivation
outline.gist: Asked why they want change, many say repentance, which is his own motivation every year: resolving that this year will be better.

outline.heading: Paradise adorns itself for Ramadan
outline.gist: His teacher sifted the many weak Ramadan narrations for their authentic phrases, among them that Paradise beautifies itself for Ramadan from year to year.

outline.heading: A paradise in this world
outline.gist: His teacher read it as also meaning the serenity of Ramadan nights, the nearest thing to Paradise on earth, which no wealth or leisure can buy.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a reset
outline.gist: Self-discipline and a reset button: forget the past year, wipe the slate clean and try again.

outline.heading: The month that changed Muslim history
outline.gist: Many decisive moments in Muslim history came in Ramadan, which has always been a safe haven for turning things around.

outline.heading: What you need from yourself
outline.gist: Name what you control: consistency, time management, discipline, understanding the Quran; people internalise habits and experiences differently, so find your own blocker.

outline.heading: Act on your own answer
outline.gist: If understanding the Quran would help, attend tafsir sessions alongside the rituals; put the month on a whiteboard and plan around exams and deadlines.

outline.heading: Strong will is not for sale
outline.gist: Will cannot be bought; it is reached through good companionship and the right environment, such as the masjid.

outline.heading: Eat light and stick to the nearest masjid
outline.gist: A heavy iftar makes the night prayer unbearable; come light and early to whichever masjid is closest, since consistency over thirty days matters most.

outline.heading: Ranking Ramadan goals
outline.gist: The audience ranks presence with Allah, the Quran, the masjid, community, setting the deen in order, bad habits and prayer.

outline.heading: Ramadan breaks bad habits
outline.gist: He cannot rid you of bad habits but Ramadan can: it is a large adjustment that wrecks the old routine through suhur, fasting and busy nights.

outline.heading: Ramadan is Ramadan because of the Quran
outline.gist: The month and Laylat al-Qadr take their rank from the Quran revealed in them, so connecting with it rightly tops the list.

outline.heading: Practical ways to connect with the Quran
outline.gist: Follow the full recitation with a translation, set a daily portion to your level, reflect on it and memorise; as a child Ramadan was his most productive month of memorising.

outline.heading: Gates open and hearts called
outline.gist: Heaven's gates open, Hell's close, the devils are chained and a caller invites seekers of good, so hundreds of millions fill masjids on the first night.

outline.heading: Presence with Allah does not come cheap
outline.gist: Connection with Allah is the most valuable thing there is; it takes commitment and consistency, maybe for years, but Allah will grant it to those who show they want it.

outline.heading: You are only as strong as your community
outline.gist: Community involvement ranked last, yet Islam is a team game: a star player on a losing team still loses, so lift those around you.

outline.heading: Why pray in congregation?
outline.gist: Connection with Allah seems private, yet Islam asks you to pursue it in a group, because it is a collective effort.

outline.heading: Look for your heart in the Quran
outline.gist: Interest in the Quran delights him; a classical saying urges seeking your heart in the Quran and weeping if it is not there.

outline.heading: The Quran will save us again
outline.gist: The Quran rescued the ummah before and is its path back to stability and dignity.

outline.heading: Focus on fasting properly
outline.gist: Most of Ramadan's reward lies in how you fast; studying, working or serving while fasting all earn reward as long as it is not sinful.

outline.heading: Fajr in congregation, then Quran
outline.gist: You are already awake for suhur, so pray Fajr in the masjid and use the early morning for your daily recitation rather than the tired hours before iftar.

outline.heading: Pray the full night prayer
outline.gist: Young people should attend the full prayer; the Prophet led long nights of recitation, stopping only lest it become obligatory.

outline.heading: Raising the standard
outline.gist: He dreams of a masjid with two completions as in his childhood; aiming for excellence draws people up, while accepting mediocrity lowers everyone, though it must be done gently.

outline.heading: Point one: repent from a way of life
outline.gist: Beyond specific sins, repent from a whole attitude and worldview and resolve to live differently.

outline.heading: The tide turns in Ramadan
outline.gist: Name the sins you worry about, but use the opening moment to turn a new leaf; good deeds are made easier and bad deeds harder this month.

outline.heading: Paradise is expensive
outline.gist: Paradise calls those who want it, but it is Allah's price and does not come cheaply.

outline.heading: Make yourself an endowment for Allah
outline.gist: Stamp yourself as waqf, dedicated to Allah and His creation for the month and then for life; Allah has already bought your life and wealth for Paradise, you just sign on.

outline.heading: Volunteering keeps the reward of prayer
outline.gist: If you would otherwise be praying behind the imam, serving at the door or outside earns both rewards; if you would have been home, only the service counts.

outline.heading: Schedule volunteers to pray too
outline.gist: Volunteers still deserve to pray; the Prophet taught that those held back by illness share the reward of those who went.

outline.heading: Joy is in giving
outline.gist: If receiving a gift still pleases you more than giving one, you have not yet learned Islam; Ramadan slows consumerism so you can find joy in feeding others.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr on the hijrah
outline.gist: Thirsty in the desert, they found milk at a tent; Abu Bakr said the Prophet drank until he himself felt satisfied.

outline.heading: The gate of quenched thirst
outline.gist: Ar-Rayyan, the gate for true fasters, means thirst quenched: every lack carried through life, emotional or material, will be filled.

outline.heading: Invest in your salah
outline.gist: Salah is not a burden but five daily meetings with the King of kings to bring your pain, hopes and fears.

outline.heading: Practice until one moment of bliss
outline.gist: Ramadan's extra prayers are practice; one prostration or dua that touches the heart, where you wish the imam would not rise, stays with you for life.

outline.heading: Interlude
Fasting is Mine and I reward it
outline.gist: Every deed has a calculable reward except fasting, which Allah rewards personally because His servant left desire, food and drink for Him; the faster has two joys.

outline.heading: The faster's breath
outline.gist: The faster's breath is sweeter to Allah than musk because any sacrifice for Him is beautiful as evidence of commitment.

outline.heading: The first night of Ramadan
outline.gist: Devils are chained, Heaven's gates opened and Hell's shut, a caller summons, and Allah frees people from the Fire every night.

outline.heading: Fasting as a shield
outline.gist: No obscenity, gossip or quarrels; 'I am fasting' is a reminder to yourself, since you fast with eyes, ears, tongue and mind.

outline.heading: Outro
Musa hastening to his Lord
outline.gist: Musa rushed ahead of his people to the appointment, saying they were following and he hastened to please Allah; that is the motto of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Outro
